opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a question I think about a lot, partly because I've had the chance to talk with a fair number of researchers coming out of Chinese labs and universities, and partly because the contrast tells you something about our own culture here.

The first thing that stands out to me is how much the younger Chinese researchers I meet are motivated by the craft itself. There's a real focus on building things that work and getting the details right: the data pipelines, the training stability, the infrastructure efficiency. You saw that with DeepSeek and with Qwen. A lot of the impressive work is careful, unglamorous engineering done extremely well under constraints, especially compute constraints. That kind of pressure produces a certain mindset. You can't just throw ten times more GPUs at a problem, so you get creative about the system.

In Silicon Valley, the outlook is often more grandiose, sometimes in a good way. People talk in terms of AGI timelines, civilizational stakes, and who's going to "win." There's a lot of narrative and a lot of philosophy attached to the work, and that drives ambition and fundraising. But it can also mean the conversation drifts away from the actual technical problems toward positioning and storytelling.

The other big difference is openness. Many of the Chinese labs have leaned heavily into releasing open-weight models, and the researchers I talk to see that as a natural way to build reputation and contribute to a global scientific community. In the US, the frontier labs have mostly gone closed, and the open ecosystem has had to fight for attention and funding. That's part of why I've been so vocal about American open models: I don't want the default open foundation that researchers around the world build on to come only from China. That's not a knock on the Chinese researchers at all. They're doing excellent work. It's more a statement about where US incentives have pushed us.

I'd add one caveat: it's easy to romanticize either side. Chinese researchers face real pressures too, including intense competition, long hours, and a different relationship with government priorities. And plenty of people in the Valley are deeply technical and humble about what they don't know. But if I had to summarize, I'd say young Chinese researchers often seem more pragmatic and execution-focused, more willing to share openly, and less caught up in the mythology of AI. Silicon Valley has more of the big-vision energy and the capital to back it up. Ideally, the field gets the best of both.

r006.rationale: It contrasts Chinese researchers’ focus on building things that work and careful engineering with Silicon Valley’s greater emphasis on grand narratives and positioning.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I get asked a lot, and I want to be careful, because my sample is skewed. I mostly interact with Chinese researchers through papers, through open-weight model releases, and through the people who've come through labs like AI2 or who I meet at conferences. So I'm seeing a filtered slice.

With that caveat, a few things stand out. The first is a kind of earnestness about the engineering. When I read the DeepSeek or Qwen technical reports, or talk to people working on them, there's a sense that the work itself is the point. They'll spend pages on how they got the training run to be stable, how they handled the data, what the exact loss curves looked like. In the Valley, a lot of that detail has been pulled out of the public conversation. The frontier labs here treat it as proprietary, and the people who have it mostly can't talk. So from the outside it can look like Chinese researchers are more open, when some of that is just a difference in what's allowed to be shared and what the incentives are for sharing it.

The second thing is ambition framed differently. In Silicon Valley the framing is very much about the frontier, about being the one to get there first, about AGI timelines, sometimes about a kind of mission narrative. The Chinese researchers I encounter tend to talk more about catching up and then about efficiency. How do you get the same capability with less compute, with restricted hardware, with a smaller team. That constraint has been really generative for them. A lot of the interesting optimizations in the last year came out of people who had to be clever because they couldn't just buy more chips.

And then there's the career texture, which is maybe underrated. A lot of young researchers in China are in a much more intense, more competitive environment. The hours are long, the talent pool is enormous, and there's less of the cushion that someone at a well-funded US lab has. That shows up as a certain hunger. People in the Valley are hungry too, but it's a different flavor, more tied to equity and status and being at the right company.

Where I'd push back on the common narrative is the idea that one side is more creative and the other is more about execution. I don't think that holds up anymore. Some of the most original research ideas of the past couple of years, things like the reasoning training recipes that got everyone talking, came out of Chinese labs. And honestly, the thing I notice most is how much the two groups are reading each other. The intellectual outlook is converging faster than the politics would suggest.

astra-6.text:
I’d be careful about generalizing, because the researchers I interact with are a pretty selective sample. But one distinction I find useful is between the questions people are curious about and the incentives around them. Young researchers in China and Silicon Valley can be interested in very similar technical problems, while having different views about which problems they can realistically pursue.

In Silicon Valley, there’s a strong tendency to connect research to a company, a product, or a story about AGI. That can make people ambitious and willing to take risks, but it can also narrow the conversation: everyone starts asking the same questions because those are the questions attracting funding and attention.

So I’d be hesitant to describe this as a fundamental intellectual difference between Chinese and American researchers. I’d want to ask what their institutions reward, what resources they can access, and how much freedom they have to follow an idea. Those things shape someone’s outlook enormously.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d be careful about generalizing. I don’t have a representative view of young Chinese AI researchers, and Silicon Valley itself has a lot of different intellectual cultures. Among researchers, there’s a shared excitement about what these models can do and a shared interest in the technical questions.

What stands out in Silicon Valley is how quickly those questions become a conversation about AGI, startups, and how the world might change. That environment rewards very ambitious predictions. But I wouldn’t take differences in how people talk publicly as a straightforward measure of their curiosity or ambition. You also have to ask what their institutions reward, what resources they have, and what they feel comfortable saying.
